title: XOM stock fluctuates near $155 as oil volatility pressures energy sector gains - eciks.org
content:
Exxon Mobil (XOM) stock fluctuated near the $155 level on May 26, 2026, reflecting broader energy sector turbulence as crude oil prices swung between $114 and $137 per barrel amid persistent geopolitical tensions. The stock’s recent trading range highlights the sector’s exposure to oil volatility, a pattern that has pressured energy stocks despite strong fundamental performance from major integrated producers. The energy sector entered May 2026 facing a complex backdrop of rising crude oil supplies, geopolitical tensions, and shifting market expectations. Brent crude traded in a wide range of $114 to $137 per barrel throughout May, according to market sources, with the volatility driven primarily by regional tensions in the Middle East and ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran. This uncertainty has created headwinds for energy stocks, even those with strong underlying cash generation. Exxon Mobil‘s stock performance reflects this broader dynamic. While the company reported solid operational results, the volatility in crude markets has prevented the stock from sustaining gains despite fundamental strength. The EIA (Energy Information Administration) expects global oil inventories to decline by 8.5 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026, suggesting tight supply dynamics that could eventually support higher prices. However, this longer-term perspective has not yet lifted near-term market sentiment. Exxon Mobil reported first-quarter 2026 earnings of $4.2 billion, or $1.00 per diluted share, representing a significant decline from $7.7 billion in Q1 2025. However, the company’s revenue climbed 4.8% to $85.14 billion, indicating strong top-line performance despite operational pressures. The earnings decline was driven primarily by unfavorable estimated timing effects of $3.9 billion and refining segment losses, which typically correlate with narrower crack spreads (the profit margin between crude oil and refined products). The company generated approximately $8.9 billion in cash flow from operations in Q1 2026, though free cash flow fell to $2.7 billion—significantly below the $8.8 billion reported in the prior-year quarter. This decline reflects increased capital expenditures of $6.2 billion as Exxon Mobil continues investing in high-return projects. Management attributes the earnings compression partly to temporary refining headwinds, suggesting potential recovery as utilization rates stabilize and crack spreads widen. Twenty-two analysts covering Exxon Mobil maintain a constructive view despite recent volatility. The consensus price target ranges from $130.00 to $185.00, with the median estimate around $169.50, suggesting meaningful upside from current levels. Bernstein (rated May 11, 2026) set a price target of $182.00, reflecting confidence in the company’s ability to navigate market cycles. The broader theme among analysts emphasizes that oil majors will prioritize resilient cash generation over aggressive production growth, aligning with Exxon Mobil‘s capital allocation discipline. The dividend remains a key attraction for income investors. The company declared a second-quarter 2026 dividend of $0.89 per share, continuing its track record of sustained capital returns. This forward dividend yield of approximately 2.66% provides a stable income stream independent of crude price fluctuations, making XOM appealing for portfolio investors seeking energy exposure with yield protection. The fundamental backdrop for energy stocks remains complex. Reuters reported on May 11, 2026, that oil majors are bracing for prolonged turbulence in energy markets, curbing enthusiasm for aggressive spending increases despite temporary price spikes. According to market analysis, Brent crude fluctuated between $114 and $137 in May amid ongoing Iran-US negotiations, which could significantly alter global supply dynamics if a nuclear agreement is reached and sanctions are lifted. The Strait of Hormuz remains a critical chokepoint, with roughly 21% of global petroleum transiting through the waterway. Regional tensions create supply premium volatility that disproportionately impacts shorter-term stock performance, even if fundamental demand remains solid. Crypto Briefing reported on May 26, 2026, that WTI crude oil futures showed only a 5.0% probability of reaching $150 by month-end, down from 7.0% the previous day—indicating fading panic premium as negotiations advance. Exxon Mobil‘s stock faces headwinds despite generating nearly $2.7 billion in free cash flow during Q1 2026. The explanation lies in how energy investors price volatility. title: USO, UCO, BATL, XOM Slip: Oil Dips Below $100 After Trump Says Iran Talks ‘Proceeding Nicely’ - Stocktwits
content: Major oil stocks and index funds declined in the overnight session heading into Tuesday after U.S. President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran “are proceeding nicely,” pushing crude below $100 a barrel. Shares of the United States Oil Fund (USO) and ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil ETF (UCO) slipped 4.7% and 5.4% lower, even as Battalion Oil (BATL) fell more than 6% in the overnight session at the time of writing. Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) fell more than 1%, while Trio Petroleum Corp. (TPET) and Indonesia Energy Corp Ltd. (INDO) shares lost more than 2% each. Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday that negotiations with Iran “are proceeding nicely!” but added, “It will only be a Great Deal for all or, no Deal at all — Back to the Battlefront and shooting, but bigger and stronger than ever before — And nobody wants that!” Oil futures were below $100 a barrel on hopes for a deal, with Brent crude futures expiring in July trading at around $98.12 a barrel at the time of writing, while WTI crude futures expiring in June slipped more than 5%, trading around $91.71 a barrel. The comments come amid reports of an Iranian delegation traveling to Qatar for consultations with senior officials to negotiate a deal with the U.S. to end the war. A report from Al Jazeera has noted that Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, and Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati are in Doha to discuss sticking points for the potential deal that could end the U.S.-Israel war on Iran. Trump had said earlier on Monday that an agreement with Iran must be “meaningful” for a deal to be reached. The president has insisted that Iran must give up its nuclear power for a deal, while Tehran has said that at this stage, Iran and the U.S. have not been “talking about the nuclear issue.” Reports have also indicated that the U.S. and Iran are discussing a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz roughly 30 days after a deal is finalized, with Iran expected to remove mines from the waterway to ensure safe maritime passage, according to Nikkei. Meanwhile, the U.S. military carried out what it described as “self-defense strikes” in southern Iran, targeting Iranian missile installations and boats allegedly attempting to deploy mines in the strait. Robin Brooks, a Senior Fellow at The Brookings Institution and a former chief FX strategist and managing director at Goldman Sachs, thinks oil prices will normalize as the critical waterway opens. “It'll obviously take time for shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz to normalize, but don't fall into the trap of thinking this means oil prices will stay high. Markets are forward-looking, so they'll price normalization long before it happens…” he said in a post on X. Meanwhile, Mohamed El-Erian, Chief Economic Advisor at Allianz, noted oil’s slip below $100 a barrel, adding that prices would depend on peace deal negotiations and traffic flow through the strait. “Brent crude is now trading well below $100 a barrel. Where this crucial price goes next will depend not only on whether the agreement is finalized but also on the details and what they imply for sustainability—particularly with respect to the return of free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz,” he said in a post on X. However, Barclays has said that it expects Brent crude oil to be around $100 for 2026, while also warning that price risks are skewed higher. Meanwhile, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projects Brent crude prices to average about $106 per barrel in May and June, citing expectations that global oil inventories will decline by roughly 8.5 million barrels per day during the second quarter of 2026. The agency also said that increasing oil output from the Middle East is likely to push crude prices down to an average of $89 per barrel by the fourth quarter of 2026, with prices easing further to around $79 per barrel in 2027. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment toward USO, BATL, and XOM was in the ‘bearish’ territory, while UCO sentiment was in the ‘bullish’ territory at the time of writing. Message volumes were in the ‘high’ levels for UCO, while they were ‘normal’ for USO and XOM. Messages for BATL were ‘extremely low’ at the time of writing. One user said, “The price of oil is showing you that Iran has nothing. Last week was a chance to sell above 100. This week above 90. Soon, Brent will be under 90. There are very few real oil bulls left in this market, it’s primarily retards. After the falling knife I may pick a spot to buy some oil, but it really is a dead trade.” USO has more than doubled so far this year, while UCO has gained more than 145% so far in 2026. BATL shares have surged more than 58%, while XOM has gained by over 26% in the same time. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. BJ's Wholesale Club Holdings (BJ) faced scrutiny from Wall Street after two firms lowered their price targets on the warehouse retailer following its fiscal first-quarter (Q1) earnings report on Friday. BJ's Wholesale Club stock tumbled 8.3% on Friday, its worst day in nine months, after investors aggressively sold shares even as the company’s Q1 earnings beat Street estimates. Analysts and investors ignored the headline numbers and instead focused on weaker underlying trends tied to merchandise demand, margin pressure and unchanged annual guidance. Citi reduced its price target on BJ’s to $100 from $118 while maintaining a ‘Buy’ rating on the stock. Analysts cited weaker merchandise margin trends during the quarter and declining valuation multiples across the retail sector. However, the new price target still implied a 15% upside potential to the stock’s closing price on Friday. Bank of America also lowered its price target on BJ’s shares, trimming it to $100 from $110 while keeping a ‘Neutral’ rating. The firm acknowledged that BJ’s exceeded quarterly expectations through stronger sales and disciplined expense management, but warned that several near-term challenges could limit future earnings upgrades. Analysts were concerned about weaker merchandise profits during the quarter. Retailers are still dealing with high shipping and supply chain costs, while heavy discounting and competitive pricing are putting more pressure on profit margins. In the Q1 earnings call, BJ's Wholesale Club Chairman and CEO Robert Eddy said gas prices rose sharply during the quarter, making it harder for customers to manage household expenses. “Gas prices remain elevated, and that pressure is real for families. To put this in further context, in April alone, our members spent $143 million more at our pumps than they did a year ago. That's equivalent to approximately 3.5% in merchandise comp dollars,” said Eddy. Eddy added that lower-income households are feeling greater financial pressure as rising costs continue to strain their budgets. BJ's Q1 net profit fell to $142.7 million from $149.8 million last year. The merchandise gross margin, excluding fuel sales and membership fee revenue, declined by roughly 10 basis points. The classification is significant because hundreds of institutional investors, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and mutual funds, base their portfolio allocations on these index classifications. As a result, any rebalancing can trigger large shifts in fund holdings, potentially triggering moves in the stocks in question. The Russell 1000 Index tracks the 1,000 largest publicly traded U.S. companies and represents the vast majority of the U.S. stock market’s total value, making it a key benchmark for large-cap investing. Meanwhile, Micron said on Friday it would invest more than $2 billion to expand and modernize its memory chip manufacturing facility in Manassas, Virginia, and has started production of its 1α DRAM chip, which it described as the most advanced memory chip ever manufactured in the U.S. Despite strong business forecasts, the sharp run-up in memory stocks has left investors questioning how much upside remains. The Nasdaq Composite added about 50 points to end the session 0.19% higher. U.S. markets were closed on Monday in observance of Memorial Day. However, the U.S. military conducted “self-defense strikes” on southern Iran, targeting Iranian missile sites and boats attempting to place mines. Chief executive Jensen Huang told investors on Nvidia’s ($NVDA) earnings call that customers are on track to spend $3 to $4 trillion on AI infrastructure by the end of the decade. According to Michael Parekh, a former Goldman Sachs executive who now runs the AI: Return to Zero Substack, the number is probably conservative, and a single company in Taiwan gets to decide whether it happens. “That they are the gating factor,” Parekh said of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) in an exclusive Stocktwits interview with Michele Steele. “Jensen’s flying to Taiwan almost every month, basically telling his friends at TSMC: please, here’s another hundred billion, make me extra fabs. But the TSMC guys are not doing it.” “TSMC is the Federal Reserve of the global tech market. They have to ramp up their manufacturing fabs, which takes three to five years to build, billions and tens and hundreds of billions of dollars. And they’re not ramping up production their to accommodate the full five-plus trillion [potential].” – Michael Parekh, Founder, AI: Return to Zero Substack NVDA’s stock closed Friday nearly 2% lower, and is down over 6% for the week. Retail sentiment around the tech giant on Stocktwits trended in ‘extremely bullish’ territory over the past week, accompanied by ‘extremely high’ levels of chatter. TSMC makes approximately 90% of the chips Nvidia needs. Apple and Nvidia together account for roughly 50% of TSMC’s revenues. When Jensen Huang stood outside a Taipei restaurant in February and told the press, “TSMC needs to work very hard this year because I need a lot of wafers,” he was describing a constraint, not a negotiation. Meanwhile, TSMC’s deliberate pacing is not stubbornness, according to Parekh. It is the rational behavior of a company that understands building a new leading-edge fab costs tens of billions of dollars and takes three to five years to reach full production. According to him, TSMC is threading the needle between the demand it can see and the capacity it can responsibly build. According Parekh, the way technology has evolved over the past year has substantially changed the demand side of things. He noted that twelve months ago, the primary use case for AI compute was chatbots. Today it is agents and reasoning models, which are systems that use more than 100 times the chips for inference that chatbots require for the same task. He stated that the acceleration in demand is what gives Jensen the confidence to cite numbers that would have sounded absurd three years ago. It is also what makes the TSMC constraint more acute rather than less, because demand is growing faster than any fab can be built to meet it. “Jensen has the confidence to talk about trillions of demand, and yes, he does have the visibility to trillions of demand. The AI was, just a year ago, all about chatbots. Now it’s about agents and reasoning, and those things use 100-plus times the chips for inference than we needed for chatbots just a year ago.”  – Michael Parekh, Founder, AI: Return to Zero Substack Parekh has covered the internet, mobile, cloud, and every major technology wave of the past three decades. He told Stocktwits this is bigger than all of them. Jensen’s $3 to $4 trillion figure, he said, is probably an underestimate. He pegged the real number at $4 to $5 trillion over the next six years, provided TSMC can build the capacity to support it. “This is way bigger than the internet boom. And Jensen is right – at least three-plus trillion. The reality is he could probably sell four to five trillion in the next six years. But the gating factor is TSMC,” Parekh stated. NVDA’s stock has gained over 13% this year, and rallied more than 60% in the past 12 months. Read also: EXCLUSIVE: A Former Goldman Sachs Executive Thinks Nvidia’s China Story Isn’t Over For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com Nvidia’s (NVDA) revenue from China remained at zero during the first quarter, but Michael Parekh, a former Goldman Sachs executive who now runs the AI: Return to Zero Substack and has covered every major technology wave since the internet era, told Stocktwits that the number is not the whole story. According to him, if a September White House meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump results in an official green light for Nvidia chip sales to China, analysts who currently model China revenue at zero would be forced to rebuild their forecasts from scratch. "If there is an official green light from Xi and China and Trump that Nvidia can trade their chips, then yes, the stock will be re-rated," Parekh told Stocktwits in an exclusive interview with Michele Steele. "People will now officially put more numbers on Nvidia's side for China, because the market is huge." Nvidia has been excluding China from its forward guidance entirely since the H20 export restrictions. Any formal resumption of official sales would require analysts to rebuild a revenue line from a stated baseline of zero, Parekh said. He added that the re-rating wouldn’t be gradual, but immediate and considerably higher. "Having said that, I'm not expecting it," Parekh said. "And Jensen's being very careful to just take those expectations down to zero." “If things were like they were a couple of years ago, there would probably be another $10 billion in here from China,” Parekh told Stocktwits. “China is the second largest market for AI, and right now Nvidia is shut out.” However, he noted that zero revenue directly from China doesn’t mean that the country doesn’t have access to Nvidia’s chips. “China is getting a lot of Nvidia chips through a lot of sources. These are porous markets. There is an indirect Nvidia China revenue line — it’s just not the official one. And that’s what we’re talking about here,” Parekh stated. He added that Chinese AI companies have been establishing subsidiaries across Singapore, Malaysia, and other Asian markets where access to Nvidia compute is less restricted. The firms legally purchase chips within their jurisdictions and make them available to Chinese companies. China has been pushing Huawei to build its own chips so the country can decouple entirely and no longer need Nvidia. In a recent interview with CNBC, chief executive Jensen Huang even said that Nvidia has “largely conceded” China’s artificial intelligence chip market to Huawei. However, according to Parekh, the ground reality is that Huawei's domestically produced chips are one to three generations behind Nvidia's current products. Moreover, CUDA, Nvidia's open-source software framework, built and refined over 19 years, is used by millions of engineers globally and is compatible with virtually every major AI model. Parekh said an engineer working with Nvidia chips can have a model running within days or weeks. "If I want to use Huawei chips to do this, I will probably need another 6, 8, 12 months to build the software framework for those chips to work with my applications," he said. Parekh estimated that China won’t be able to shed its reliance on Nvidia for at least another five years. "They don't have access to the chip-making equipment, they're behind, and that will take five to ten years. title: Is ExxonMobil's Guyana Expansion a Game-Changer for XOM Stock - Kavout
content: ExxonMobil (NYSE: XOM) is at a pivotal juncture with its ambitious offshore development plans in Guyana, particularly as it navigates the environmental approval process for the Longtail and Haimara projects. The company's recent submission of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for Longtail and the subsequent public consultations, which began on April 13, 2026, mark a crucial step toward unlocking significant future production. This move is not merely procedural; it represents a strategic doubling down on one of the world's most promising new oil frontiers, potentially reshaping XOM's long-term growth trajectory and shareholder value. However, the path is fraught with environmental and regulatory challenges that demand careful consideration from investors. The proposed Longtail development, ExxonMobil's eighth in the Stabroek Block, is projected to begin production in 2030 and operate for approximately 30 years. This long-term horizon underscores the strategic importance of Guyana to ExxonMobil's portfolio, especially given the project's substantial output estimates of 1.2 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day and around 250,000 barrels per day of condensate. With XOM currently trading at $154.92 as of May 22, 2026, and a market capitalization of $642.14 billion, the successful sanctioning and development of these projects are essential to fuel future earnings growth, particularly against a backdrop of -4.5% year-over-year revenue decline in FY2025. The ongoing public consultations, led by ExxonMobil Guyana President Alistair Routledge, aim to address community concerns and integrate feedback into the EIA process, a critical component for securing final authorization from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The Longtail and Haimara projects are cornerstones of ExxonMobil's aggressive expansion strategy in Guyana's Stabroek Block, a prolific offshore basin that has yielded numerous world-class discoveries. ExxonMobil operates the Stabroek Block with a 45% interest, alongside partners Hess (now owned by Chevron) with 30% and CNOOC with 25%. This consortium has transformed Guyana into a major global oil producer in a remarkably short period, with Longtail representing the eighth and Haimara the expected ninth development within this block. The sheer scale of these developments is staggering; Longtail alone is designed to produce 250,000 barrels per day of condensate and 1.2 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas, contributing significantly to global energy supply for decades. These projects are strategically located in what ExxonMobil Guyana President Alistair Routledge refers to as the "southeast gas area" of the Stabroek Block. Longtail is positioned as the anchor for several discoveries in its vicinity, while Haimara is slated to anchor the subsequent project. The company submitted the Field Development Plan (FDP) for Longtail by the end of March 2026, signaling its readiness to move forward once environmental authorizations are secured. The projected start of production in 2030 for Longtail, with an operational lifespan of roughly 30 years, provides a clear long-term revenue stream for ExxonMobil, bolstering its upstream segment and providing a hedge against potential declines in mature assets elsewhere. For ExxonMobil, these developments are crucial for maintaining its production profile and driving future cash flow, especially as the company navigates a dynamic global energy landscape. The Stabroek Block discoveries have been instrumental in XOM's recent performance, and continued success here is vital for offsetting the -23.1% year-over-year decline in free cash flow observed in FY2025. The consistent stream of new projects, each requiring substantial capital investment but promising high returns, underpins the company's commitment to its fossil fuel portfolio while also acknowledging the increasing demand for natural gas as a transition fuel. The successful execution of Longtail and Haimara will solidify Guyana's role as a core growth engine for ExxonMobil for the foreseeable future. The successful development of the Longtail and Haimara projects in Guyana holds profound implications for ExxonMobil's financial outlook, promising to inject substantial revenue and cash flow into the company's operations starting in 2030. With Longtail alone projected to add 250,000 barrels per day of condensate and 1.2 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas, these volumes represent a significant boost to XOM's overall production capacity. This increased output is critical for a company that saw its revenue decline by -4.5% year-over-year in FY2025 and net income fall by -14.4% during the same period. The new production streams are expected to reverse these trends, providing a much-needed catalyst for top-line and bottom-line growth. From a valuation perspective, ExxonMobil currently trades at a P/E ratio of 25.60, which is relatively high for an integrated oil major, suggesting that investors are already anticipating future growth from projects like those in Guyana. The company's TTM EPS stands at $6.05, and the expected production from Longtail, operating for 30 years, will contribute significantly to future earnings per share. While the immediate impact on financials is still several years away, the certainty of these projects moving forward, contingent on environmental approvals, provides a strong long-term investment thesis. The company's dividend yield of 2.6%, with a payout ratio of 68.1%, is supported by its robust cash generation, which these new projects are designed to enhance further. Moreover, the sheer scale of the Stabroek Block's reserves and the continuous stream of new developments offer a long runway for capital allocation and shareholder returns. The $642.14 billion market cap reflects ExxonMobil's dominant position, but sustained growth requires consistent project execution. The Longtail project's contribution to free cash flow, which saw a -23.1% decline in FY2025, will be vital for improving financial flexibility, funding future exploration, and potentially increasing shareholder distributions. The company's relatively low debt-to-equity ratio of 0.19 and a net debt-to-EBITDA of 0.65 provide ample capacity to finance these large-scale developments, underscoring a disciplined financial approach even as it pursues aggressive growth in Guyana. ExxonMobil's ambitious development plans in Guyana, while promising significant returns, are not without substantial environmental and regulatory hurdles. The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) process for the Longtail project, which commenced public consultations on April 13, 2026, is a critical phase that requires addressing concerns from local communities and environmental advocates. ExxonMobil Guyana President Alistair Routledge emphasized the importance of these 60-day consultations, stating they are designed to allow residents to review studies and raise concerns, ensuring risks are mitigated. However, past experiences suggest that public engagement in Guyana's EIA process has been limited, with a lack of public awareness and understanding often leading to insufficient feedback, as highlighted in a critical review of the process. A major point of contention revolves around oil spill liability. A June 2023 decision by an appeals court ordered ExxonMobil to put up $2 billion for Guyana oil spill costs, but critically, it shifted the remaining uncapped liability onto the Guyanese people. This decision, which followed a lower court ruling that had initially held ExxonMobil fully responsible, has been widely criticized by organizations like the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) for exposing Guyana to significant financial risk. The 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill, which cost BP and its insurers $70 billion, serves as a stark reminder of the potential scale of such disasters, far exceeding the $2 billion bond. This lack of full financial assurance from ExxonMobil's parent company remains a significant environmental and reputational risk. Furthermore, the legal framework governing oil and gas in Guyana has been described as evolving. The Environmental Protection Act of 1996, initially lacked specific guidelines for the oil and gas sector, which only emerged as a major industry after ExxonMobil's Liza-1 discovery in May 2015. While the EPA now requires EIAs for projects like Longtail, concerns persist about the sufficiency of consultation periods and the adequacy of addressing social and cultural issues. The company's own Oil Spill Response Plan for Guyana Operations, last revised in December 2025, outlines safeguards, but the ongoing debate about liability and transparency, particularly regarding the actual terms and scope of insurance coverage, continues to cast a shadow over ExxonMobil's operations in the region. Guyana has rapidly become an indispensable pillar of ExxonMobil's global strategy, representing one of the most significant growth engines for the energy giant. The Stabroek Block discoveries, initiated with Liza-1 in 2015, have transformed the country into a crucial source of future production, particularly as the company navigates a complex energy transition and seeks to maintain its competitive edge. With an operational interest of 45% in the Stabroek Block, ExxonMobil is heavily invested in unlocking the vast hydrocarbon potential of this region, which is expected to underpin its upstream segment for decades. The Longtail and Haimara projects, slated for production starting in 2030 and operating for 30 years, are central to this long-term vision. The strategic importance of Guyana is amplified by its role in diversifying ExxonMobil's asset base and providing high-margin barrels. Unlike some mature fields that face declining production and higher operating costs, Guyana offers prolific, low-cost production that enhances XOM's overall profitability and resilience. This focus on high-quality, advantaged assets is a core tenet of CEO Darren W. Woods' strategy, aiming to improve capital efficiency and shareholder returns. The projected output of 250,000 barrels per day from Longtail alone, combined with substantial natural gas volumes, will contribute significantly to ExxonMobil's global production targets and cash flow generation, which is crucial given the -5.5% decline in operating cash flow in FY2025. Moreover, Guyana's emergence as a major oil producer reshapes regional energy security and offers a stable, democratic partner for the U.S. in South America. For ExxonMobil, this geopolitical stability, coupled with the sheer scale of the resource, makes Guyana an attractive investment destination despite the environmental scrutiny. The company's commitment to the region is further demonstrated by its ongoing environmental studies and community engagements, aiming to balance resource development with responsible operations. While ExxonMobil has seen its employee count decrease from 61,500 in 2023 to 58,000 in 2025, reflecting broader efficiency drives, the Guyana operations remain a key area of investment and talent deployment, signaling its enduring importance to the company's future. The investment outlook for ExxonMobil (XOM) is intrinsically linked to the successful, and environmentally responsible, development of its Guyana projects. While the Longtail and Haimara developments promise substantial long-term production and cash flow, investors must weigh this against the inherent risks. The company's current P/E ratio of 25.60 suggests that a significant portion of this future growth is already priced into the stock, which closed at $154.92 on May 22, 2026. The market is clearly optimistic about Guyana's potential, but any delays in environmental approvals, increased regulatory burdens, or significant cost overruns could temper this enthusiasm. The ongoing public consultations and the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) requirement for a full Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for Haimara underscore the heightened scrutiny. The $2 billion oil spill liability bond, while substantial, leaves Guyana financially exposed to larger catastrophic events, a risk that could eventually translate into reputational damage or increased regulatory pressure for ExxonMobil. Investors should monitor the progress of these approvals closely, as they represent critical milestones for the 2030 production target for Longtail. Despite a recent -4.5% decline in FY2025 revenue and -14.4% drop in net income, ExxonMobil's strong balance sheet, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.19, provides a solid foundation to absorb the capital expenditures required for these mega-projects. The 2.6% dividend yield remains attractive, supported by the company's long-term cash generation capabilities, which will be significantly bolstered by the 250,000 barrels per day from Longtail. For long-term investors, XOM represents a play on global energy demand and a company with a clear growth pipeline in Guyana, but the narrative will increasingly be shaped by its ability to navigate environmental and social governance challenges effectively. ExxonMobil's strategic focus on Guyana positions it for robust long-term production growth and enhanced shareholder value, provided it successfully navigates the complex environmental and regulatory landscape. The Longtail and Haimara projects are vital for XOM's future, offering a compelling growth story for investors willing to accept the associated execution and environmental risks. title: Oil Above $90: Is ExxonMobil a Better Buy Than ConocoPhillips? - The Globe and Mail

Against this backdrop, let us compare two energy giants, Exxon Mobil CorporationXOM and ConocoPhillipsCOP, to determine which stock offers a better buying opportunity now. West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) crude is trading at more than the $90-per-barrel mark. The high price is being backed by ongoing tensions in the Middle East. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (“EIA”) in its latest short-term energy outlook projected WTI at $85.68 per barrel for this year, higher than $65.40 last year. A highly favorable pricing environment for the commodity is likely to continue supporting ExxonMobil's exploration and production activities, which contribute to the majority of its earnings. To provide a glimpse of the upstream assets, the company has a massive footprint in the Permian, the most prolific oil and gas play in the United States, and offshore Guyana. In the Permian, the integrated giant has been employing lightweight proppant technology and hence is capable of boosting its well recoveries by up to as much as 20%. On the first quarter earnings call, XOM mentioned that it is staying aligned with its plan of growing its production in the most prolific basin to 1.8 million oil equivalent barrels this year. In Guyana, XOM has made several oil and gas discoveries, further highlighting its solid production outlook. Record production from both resources has been aiding its top and bottom lines. In both resources, the breakeven costs are low. With its solid portfolio of upstream assets, COP is well-positioned to gain. The upstream energy giant has low-cost drilling opportunities across Permian, Eagle Ford and Bakken that could be successfully developed over two decades. The outlook for ConocoPhillips’ upstream operations also looks highly profitable. Both ConocoPhillips and XOM have strong balance sheets that they could rely on during an unfavorable business environment. The debt-to-capitalization of ExxonMobil is only 15.44%, lower than COP’s 26.55%. Thus, both the energy giants could rely on their balance sheet strengths to run their operations smoothly when the business scenario turns unfavorable. Coming to the price chart, both ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips have had a strong run-up over the past year. Over the period, XOM has jumped 50.3%, while COP gained 41.4%. On a relative basis, XOM is trading at a 10.24x trailing 12-month Enterprise Value to Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EV/EBITDA), which is a discount compared with COP’s 6.59x. Thus, it has become evident that investors are willing to pay a premium for XOM over COP. This is because, although both XOM and COP are benefiting from the ongoing strength in oil prices, being an integrated energy player with a footprint in refining and chemicals businesses, ExxonMobil’s operation is relatively more stable, making it a better investment pick.
